newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav economy in recession, no progress seen.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav economy in recession, no progress seen.

text.p: Yugoslavia's economy is stuck in recession and will remain there until fresh foreign funds start flowing in, the Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) said on Thursday.
"April economic indicators show the economy is still in recession," IEN economist Stojan Stamenkovic told reporters.

Recession had resulted from the constant lack of capital plus inadequate economic and ownership structures and an economic policy reliant on discretionary intervention instead of macro-economic management, IEN said in its latest report.
Economists said April failed to bring an expected seasonal decline in overall industrial output due to cold weather which boosted energy production.
But other industries performed badly and economists were confident that better April results from the energy sector were only temporary.

Economists say the Yugoslav economy has been devastated by a combination of mismanagement and a lack of reform plus international sanctions imposed during the Bosnian war and hyperinflation in the early 1990s, which has since been eradicated.
IEN saw a possible financial improvement if the sale of 49 percent of the Serbian telecommunications company Telekom Srbija materialises soon.
The government remains mute about talks on selling the Telekom stake, unofficially estimated to bring at least one billion dollars in fresh capital to state coffers.
"Some improvement, but again only a short-term one, may happen if the funds are used to boost consumer demand," Stamenkovic said.
But in the long run, Yugoslavia needed to address its structural and fiscal problems, he added.
The economic policy stood at a crossroads. It needed to pursue currency and price stability but also boost production, IEN said.
Tight monetary control was vital for price and currency stability, but companies remained without working capital and had no possibility to increase sales on export markets.
"Both monetary and fiscal policy create deflationary pressures not allowing industrial production to revive.
"There is a vicious circle. By reducing demand, any destabilisation of prices and the dinar rate is prevented, but this begins to choke production," the IEN report said.

Yugoslavia's economy could escape from this trap only if it got external financial support, but the problem had to be dealt with by politicians as well. Foreign funds were not an option as long as an outer wall of sanctions remained in place.

Economists cautioned that Yugoslavia did not use the chance it had in 1994 when it started from scratch by launching a new dinar at par to the German mark after a year of one of the world's highest rates of inflation.

"The monetary reconstruction programme, launched late in January 1994, fell short of dealing with a public spending deficit which stood at 14 percent of GDP at the time," IEN head Tomislav Popovic said.

Over the past three years the state did not tackle the problem of a flourishing grey economy and constantly delayed any structural reforms. "Those are the reasons why the Yugoslav economy remains in such a bad state," he added.

"The social, economic and psychological consequences of further delay of reforms will be immense. Whoever is in power will have to deal with that hot potato," Popovic said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
